title: The Software Spellbook — From Magical Ideas to Working Applications

learningObjectives.description: Explain software and how applications help users solve problems.
Turn a user need into clear, checkable software requirements.
Describe Plan → Build → Test → Improve → Release as an iterative development cycle.
Divide an application into manageable components with clear responsibilities.
Use testing, debugging and user feedback to check and improve software.
Explain how version control, collaboration and reviews support ongoing projects.

variants.intro: Hexi: Help me build the Great Goblin Treat Tracker! It is a pretend app for remembering my treat boxes. We will plan it, give its parts jobs, and find a story bug. No real code needed.

sections.title: An app helps with a problem
paragraphs: Software is instructions and other information a computer uses. An app is software that helps with a job. Hexi forgets which pretend box holds his treats!

sections.title: Decide what it must do
paragraphs: Our app should save a treat name and its box, then show the box when asked. That is a clear goal. Fancy music can wait.

sections.title: Plan, build, test, improve, release
paragraphs: Plan what is needed. Build a small version. Test it. Improve what is wrong, then check again. Release means share the checked version with its users. You can go around again.

sections.title: Give each part a clear job
paragraphs: One part shows the screen. One remembers treat boxes. One looks up the right box. Small parts with clear jobs are easier to change.

sections.title: Find bugs and listen to users
paragraphs: A bug is a mistake. If the app shows the wrong box, compare the answer with the treat list. Try a known treat and a missing treat. Ask users what was confusing.

sections.title: Remember changes and work together
paragraphs: A tool called Git can record chosen sets of changes, like labeled pages in our project’s history. A teammate can help review a change. A saved version can still have bugs. No account is needed here.

variants.intro: Hexi: Turn a user need into a small software project. Plan requirements, connect components, investigate a defect and distinguish proposed work from verified release evidence.

sections.title: An app helps with a problem
paragraphs: Software includes programs and related data that make computers useful. Applications solve user problems. This lesson focuses on creating and maintaining a project, beyond the earlier lesson on precise instructions.

sections.title: Decide what it must do
paragraphs: Start with user needs, then write requirements that can be checked. Our fictional tracker must save an item and location and find it later. Plan a small useful first version; optional decoration can wait. Ask questions when behavior is unclear.

sections.title: Plan, build, test, improve, release
paragraphs: Plan → Build → Test → Improve → Release describes a repeating workflow. Check what users need, build a small version, compare expected and observed results, fix and retest, then release with approval. Feedback can start another cycle.

sections.title: Give each part a clear job
paragraphs: Give screen, storage and lookup components clear responsibilities. Lookup uses saved records; the screen shows the lookup result. Decide how they communicate and what a missing result means. Small components still need integration checks.

sections.title: Find bugs and listen to users
paragraphs: A defect can make an app return the wrong location. Trace the supplied records and expected result. Choose tests for known and missing items. Debugging fixes a cause; testing checks behavior. Listen to users and retest changes. Do not claim a test passed unless a result was observed.

sections.title: Remember changes and work together
paragraphs: Git records chosen snapshots of a project through commits, so people can compare versions and understand changes. Branches can separate work, and reviews help teammates examine it before integration. Git is not the same as GitHub; this lesson needs neither an account nor a real repository. A commit or review alone does not guarantee correct software.

sections.title: An app helps with a problem
paragraphs: Software engineering includes understanding needs, designing, implementing, evaluating and maintaining software—not only writing instructions. An application supports a user task; we will plan a fictional equipment-location tracker.

sections.title: Decide what it must do
paragraphs: A functional requirement describes behavior: save an item/location and retrieve it. A nonfunctional requirement describes a quality or constraint, such as readable keyboard-accessible controls. Make both checkable. An MVP is the smallest useful scope for learning from users, not permission to skip safety, privacy or accessibility.

sections.title: Plan, build, test, improve, release
paragraphs: Plan → Build → Test → Improve → Release is a simplified iterative cycle, not a one-way waterfall rule. Agree acceptance criteria, build a small slice, test observed results, fix issues and retest before an approved release. After release, feedback, defects and changing needs drive maintenance.

sections.title: Give each part a clear job
paragraphs: Separate presentation, storage and lookup responsibilities. The lookup depends on saved records; the screen presents its result. Define their interface and expected missing-item behavior. Modular design helps isolate changes but does not automatically prevent integration bugs.

sections.title: Find bugs and listen to users
paragraphs: Testing compares actual and expected outcomes; debugging investigates and corrects a cause. Use ordinary, missing and boundary cases and retest after a fix. User feedback can reveal usability needs that passing tests miss. A proposed fix or written test is not a verified passing result.

sections.title: Remember changes and work together
paragraphs: Git records selected project snapshots through commits; it does not automatically save every keystroke or prove correctness. Compare changes, explain intent and request code review. Git is a version-control tool; GitHub is an optional hosting service, not required to use Git. Coordinate integration, handle conflicts and retain responsible review/release decisions.

practiceTasks.title: Plan a useful first version
practiceTasks.instruction: Hexi forgets his pretend treat boxes. Choose what the app needs first.
practiceTasks.goal: Help Hexi find treats without adding everything at once.
practiceTasks.input: Problem: forgotten treat boxes. Needed: save and find a treat’s box. Missing treat: what should the screen say?
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: small save/find scope; keyboard-accessible controls; clarify missing-item behavior
practiceTasks.explanation: Save and find treat boxes first. Keep the controls easy to use. Ask what to show when a treat is missing.
practiceTasks.hint: Start with the user’s need. Choose a usable first version and ask about the missing case.

slots.label: Useful first features

options.text: Save and find names and boxes
Only play decorative music
Build every imaginable feature now

slots.hint: Start with saving and finding, not decoration.

slots.label: Make the controls usable

options.text: Let people use the controls with a keyboard
Require a mouse for every action
Hide the controls behind unreadable labels

slots.hint: People need to reach and understand the controls.

slots.label: A name is missing: what next?

options.text: Ask what message should appear
Invent an answer and call it agreed
Ask for real student private records

slots.hint: That behavior is unspecified. Ask before assuming.

practiceTasks.title: Organize the workshop
practiceTasks.instruction: Give the pretend app’s parts clear jobs. Then choose the order for building and checking it.
practiceTasks.goal: Keep the jobs clear and check the app before sharing.
practiceTasks.input: Screen shows answers. Storage keeps name/location records. Lookup finds a location from storage. No build or tests have run.
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: separate screen/storage/lookup; save before lookup; plan-build-test-improve/retest-release
practiceTasks.explanation: The screen shows, storage remembers, and lookup finds. Save a box before looking it up. Plan, build, test, improve and check again before sharing.
practiceTasks.hint: Which part shows, remembers or finds? What must exist before lookup can use it?

slots.label: Choose the parts’ jobs

options.text: Screen shows; storage remembers; lookup finds
Every part changes every other part without clear jobs
Only a screen; nothing remembers records

slots.hint: Give each part one clear responsibility.

slots.label: Respect the dependency

options.text: Save a name and box, then look it up
Guarantee lookup works before any record exists
Remove all stored records but promise saved results

slots.hint: Lookup needs a saved record to find its location.

slots.label: Choose the project cycle

options.text: Plan → Build → Test → Improve and retest → Release
Build → Release → Maybe test later
Plan → Build → Test → Never listen to users again

slots.hint: Check and retest before release; feedback can start another cycle.

practiceTasks.title: Repair, check and review
practiceTasks.instruction: Pretend records say Moon Biscuit is in box A and Star Snack is in box B. The app always shows box A. Find the bug and choose how to check a fix.
practiceTasks.goal: Find the right box, check the fix, and keep a clear project history.
practiceTasks.input: Moon Biscuit → box A. Star Snack → box B. Bug: every search returns box A. No check of a fix has happened yet.
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: match requested name; known and missing-item tests; record/review change without claiming unobserved passes
practiceTasks.explanation: Find the name that was asked for. Check both treat names and a missing name. Keep a labeled version and ask for review. A planned check is not a passed check.
practiceTasks.hint: The second item exposes returning the first record. A test plan is not a result, and a saved version is not proof.

slots.label: Repair the bug

options.text: Find the requested name and return its own box
Keep returning the first location
Rename the app without changing lookup

slots.hint: The requested name may be the second record, not the first.

slots.label: Select a useful test set

options.text: Check both known names and the agreed missing-name message
Check the first name only
Check only decorative colors

slots.hint: The second known name catches this bug; the missing case checks agreed behavior.

slots.label: Version, review and release status

options.text: Record a labeled change, ask for review and say checks still need to run
Claim all tests passed because a fix was suggested
Erase all history and release without checking

slots.hint: Git/review can help track work. They do not turn an unrun test into a pass.
